claim: A new quantitative phase imaging method was developed for measuring intracellular density in fission yeast.
source: Here, we developed a new QPI method for measuring the intracellular density of fission yeast cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of a new QPI method.

claim: The QPI method is label-free and based on analysis of z-stacks of bright-field images.
source: This label-free method is based on the analysis of z-stacks of bright-field images (Bostan et al., 2016), thus having the advantage of not requiring a specialized phase objective or holographic system.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical basis of the method and cites Bostan et al., 2016.

claim: Dry-mass density in fission yeast is maintained in a narrow distribution.
source: Here, using a new quantitative phase imaging method, we determined that dry-mass density in fission yeast is maintained in a narrow distribution and exhibits homeostatic behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on QPI measurements.

claim: Dry-mass density exhibits homeostatic behavior in fission yeast.
source: Here, using a new quantitative phase imaging method, we determined that dry-mass density in fission yeast is maintained in a narrow distribution and exhibits homeostatic behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on QPI measurements.

claim: Density decreased during G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: However, density varied during the cell cycle, decreasing during G2, increasing in mitosis and cytokinesis, and dropping rapidly at cell birth.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the cell cycle-dependent density variations observed.

claim: Density increased during mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: However, density varied during the cell cycle, decreasing during G2, increasing in mitosis and cytokinesis, and dropping rapidly at cell birth.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the cell cycle-dependent density variations observed.

claim: Density dropped rapidly at cell birth.
source: However, density varied during the cell cycle, decreasing during G2, increasing in mitosis and cytokinesis, and dropping rapidly at cell birth.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the cell cycle-dependent density variations observed.

claim: Density variations were explained by a constant rate of biomass synthesis coupled to slowdown of volume growth during cell division and rapid expansion post-cytokinesis.
source: These density variations were explained by a constant rate of biomass synthesis, coupled to slowdown of volume growth during cell division and rapid expansion post-cytokinesis.
evidence: The abstract provides the mechanistic explanation for density variations.

claim: Arrest at specific cell-cycle stages exacerbated density changes.
source: Arrest at specific cell-cycle stages exacerbated density changes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from cell cycle arrest experiments.

claim: Spatially heterogeneous patterns of density suggested links between density regulation, tip growth, and intracellular osmotic pressure.
source: Spatially heterogeneous patterns of density suggested links between density regulation, tip growth, and intracellular osmotic pressure.
evidence: The abstract summarizes findings on spatial density patterns.

claim: Systematic density variations during the cell cycle are predominantly due to modulation of volume expansion.
source: Our results demonstrate that systematic density variations during the cell cycle are predominantly due to modulation of volume expansion, and reveal functional consequences of density gradients and cell-cycle arrests.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Intracellular density impacts the physical nature of the cytoplasm and can globally affect cellular processes.
source: Intracellular density impacts the physical nature of the cytoplasm and can globally affect cellular processes, yet density regulation remains poorly understood.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Density affects the concentration and activities of biomolecules.
source: density affects the concentration and activities of biomolecules and can impact biophysical properties of the cytoplasm such as macromolecular crowding, diffusion, mechanical stiffness, and phase transitions (Mitchison, 2019; Neurohr et al., 2019; van den Berg et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Density can impact biophysical properties of the cytoplasm such as macromolecular crowding, diffusion, mechanical stiffness, and phase transitions.
source: density affects the concentration and activities of biomolecules and can impact biophysical properties of the cytoplasm such as macromolecular crowding, diffusion, mechanical stiffness, and phase transitions (Mitchison, 2019; Neurohr et al., 2019; van den Berg et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Substantial shifts in density and/or crowding have been detected in development, aging, and disease states.
source: For example, substantial shifts in density and/or crowding have been detected in development, aging, and disease states (Neurohr and Amon, 2020; Oh et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this claim.

claim: In cultured mammalian cells, volume increases by 10–30% during mitosis.
source: Even normal cell-cycle progression can involve changes in density; in cultured mammalian cells, volume increases by 10–30% during mitosis (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015), which likely dilutes the cytoplasm prior to an increase in density during cytokinesis.
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this claim about mammalian cells.

claim: Volume increase during mitosis in mammalian cells likely dilutes the cytoplasm prior to an increase in density during cytokinesis.
source: Even normal cell-cycle progression can involve changes in density; in cultured mammalian cells, volume increases by 10–30% during mitosis (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015), which likely dilutes the cytoplasm prior to an increase in density during cytokinesis.
evidence: The introduction infers this consequence from cited observations.

claim: Budding yeast cells arrested in G1 phase grow to very large sizes and exhibit dilution of the cytoplasm accompanied by decreased protein synthesis and growth rate.
source: For instance, budding yeast cells that are arrested in G1 phase grow to very large sizes and exhibit dilution of the cytoplasm accompanied by decreased protein synthesis and growth rate (Neurohr et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites Neurohr et al., 2019 for this observation.

claim: Temporary inhibition of volume growth using osmotic oscillations or inhibition of secretion leads to increased density accompanied by a subsequent dramatic increase in volume growth rate in fission yeast.
source: Conversely, temporary inhibition of volume growth using osmotic oscillations or inhibition of secretion leads to increased density accompanied by a subsequent dramatic increase in volume growth rate in fission yeast (Knapp et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites Knapp et al., 2019 for this observation.

claim: Suspended microchannel resonators (SMRs) infer buoyant cell mass from changes in the frequency of a resonating cantilever as a single cell passes through an embedded microchannel.
source: Suspended microchannel resonators (SMRs) infer buoyant cell mass from changes in the frequency of a resonating cantilever as a single cell passes through an embedded microchannel (Burg et al., 2007).
evidence: The introduction describes SMR technology and cites Burg et al., 2007.

claim: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is a well-established optical technique for extracting dry-mass measurements from changes in the refractive index.
source: As an alternative to SMRs, quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is a well-established optical technique for extracting dry-mass measurements from changes in the refractive index (Park et al., 2018), as the refractive indices of major cellular components such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids are similar (Zangle and Teitell, 2014).
evidence: The introduction describes QPI and cites Park et al., 2018.

claim: The refractive indices of major cellular components such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids are similar.
source: As an alternative to SMRs, quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is a well-established optical technique for extracting dry-mass measurements from changes in the refractive index (Park et al., 2018), as the refractive indices of major cellular components such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids are similar (Zangle and Teitell, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites Zangle and Teitell, 2014 for this property.

claim: The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe is a leading cell-cycle model.
source: The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe is a leading cell-cycle model, as these rod-shaped cells have a highly regular shape, size, and cell cycle conducive to quantitative analyses (Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction states this and cites Hoffman et al., 2015.

claim: Fission yeast cells have a highly regular shape, size, and cell cycle conducive to quantitative analyses.
source: The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe is a leading cell-cycle model, as these rod-shaped cells have a highly regular shape, size, and cell cycle conducive to quantitative analyses (Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction states this and cites Hoffman et al., 2015.

claim: The mean dry-mass density of wild-type S. pombe cells growing at 30°C in rich YE5S medium was 282 ± 16 mg/mL.
source: Using this methodology, we determined that the mean dry-mass density of an asynchronous population of wild-type S. pombe cells growing at 30°C in rich YE5S medium was 282 ± 16 mg/mL (Figure 1C).
evidence: The results section reports this measurement with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The distribution of densities had a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.06.
source: Nonetheless, the distribution of densities was remarkably narrow, with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.06, despite variability in cell size and cell-cycle stage.
evidence: The results section reports this statistical measure.

claim: For cells within the same cell-cycle stage, the distribution of densities was even narrower (CV <0.05).
source: For cells within the same cell-cycle stage, the distribution of densities was even narrower (CV <0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports this with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Cell density at the beginning of the cell cycle was inversely correlated to the change in density during the cell cycle.
source: To determine whether cells could recover from fluctuations in density, we examined the change in density over a cell cycle as a function of initial density at the beginning of the cell cycle. These two quantities were inversely related (Figure 1D), indicating a homeostatic behavior that maintains density.
evidence: The results section describes this correlation with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The inverse correlation between initial density and density change indicates homeostatic behavior that maintains density.
source: These two quantities were inversely related (Figure 1D), indicating a homeostatic behavior that maintains density.
evidence: The results section interprets the correlation as evidence of homeostasis.

claim: A similar distribution of densities was observed in cells grown at 25°C and after temperature shifts.
source: A similar distribution of densities was observed in cells grown at 25°C and after temperature shifts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Density gradually decreased from the beginning of the cell cycle through G2 phase by ~5%.
source: Density gradually decreased from the beginning of the cell cycle through G2 phase by ~5%, followed by a steady rise during mitosis and cytokinesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Density showed a steady rise during mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: Density gradually decreased from the beginning of the cell cycle through G2 phase by ~5%, followed by a steady rise during mitosis and cytokinesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Dry mass increased steadily throughout the cell cycle without any obvious transitions.
source: By contrast to volume, dry mass increased steadily throughout the cell cycle without any obvious transitions (Figure 2D).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The density increase during mitosis and cytokinesis is a consequence of continued mass accumulation when volume growth halts.
source: These measurements suggest that the density increase during mitosis and cytokinesis is a consequence of continued mass accumulation when volume growth halts.
evidence: The results section infers this mechanism from the measurements.

claim: SMR measurements revealed that fission yeast exhibit a mean buoyant density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL.
source: SMR measurements revealed that fission yeast exhibit a mean buoyant density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL, and buoyant densities were lower in intermediate-sized cells than in small and large cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with our QPI-based observations of cell cycle-dependent densities (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section reports SMR measurements with reference to figures.

claim: Buoyant densities were lower in intermediate-sized cells than in small and large cells.
source: SMR measurements revealed that fission yeast exhibit a mean buoyant density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL, and buoyant densities were lower in intermediate-sized cells than in small and large cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with our QPI-based observations of cell cycle-dependent densities (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section reports SMR measurements with reference to figures.

claim: The relative changes in buoyant density were much less than changes in dry-mass density due to the different nature of the respective measurements.
source: As expected, the relative changes in buoyant density were much less than changes in dry-mass density due to the different nature of the respective measurements: dry-mass density accounts only for a fraction of buoyant density as cells are comprised mostly of water, and hence relative changes are magnified (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section explains this difference and cites Feijó Delgado et al., 2013.

claim: Dry-mass density accounts only for a fraction of buoyant density as cells are comprised mostly of water.
source: As expected, the relative changes in buoyant density were much less than changes in dry-mass density due to the different nature of the respective measurements: dry-mass density accounts only for a fraction of buoyant density as cells are comprised mostly of water, and hence relative changes are magnified (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section explains this and cites Feijó Delgado et al., 2013.

claim: At the end of cytokinesis, the middle layer of the septum is digested, and daughter cells separate.
source: At the end of cytokinesis, the middle layer of the septum is digested, and daughter cells separate (Martín-Cuadrado et al., 2003; Hercyk et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section cites references for this biological process.

claim: During cell separation, the septum bulges outward on each side to form the rounded shape of the new end, in a physical process driven by turgor pressure.
source: During this 5–10 min period, the septum bulges outward on each side to form the rounded shape of the new end, in a physical process driven by turgor pressure (Atilgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites Atilgan et al., 2015 for this process.

claim: QPI analysis showed a consistent drop in density within a 5-min window around cell separation.
source: QPI analysis of individual cells showed a consistent drop in density within a 5-min window around cell separation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); during this period, cell volume increased by ~5% while density decreased by ~5% (Figure 2F).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: During cell separation, cell volume increased by ~5% while density decreased by ~5%.
source: QPI analysis of individual cells showed a consistent drop in density within a 5-min window around cell separation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); during this period, cell volume increased by ~5% while density decreased by ~5% (Figure 2F).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The magnitude and rapidity of the density change suggest that the volume increase at cell separation is due primarily to swelling from water uptake.
source: The magnitude and rapidity of the density change suggest that the volume increase at cell separation is due primarily to swelling from water uptake.
evidence: The results section infers this mechanism from the observations.

claim: Density appears to be directly tied to the dynamics of volume expansion.
source: Thus, density appears to be directly tied to the dynamics of volume expansion.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the observations.

claim: The absolute rate of dry-mass accumulation steadily increased during the cell cycle.
source: The absolute rate of dry-mass accumulation steadily increased during the cell cycle (Figure 2D).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Dry-mass dynamics were more exponential than linear in nature.
source: Dry-mass dynamics were more exponential than linear in nature (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), as shown by a comparison of linear versus exponential fits (Figure 2G) and in the dynamics of normalized mass growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The results section reports this analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The absolute rate of mass synthesis was higher during mitosis and cytokinesis than at the beginning of the cell cycle.
source: The absolute rate of mass synthesis was therefore higher during mitosis and cytokinesis than at the beginning of the cell cycle, even though the cell slowed in volume growth late in the cycle.
evidence: The results section infers this from the exponential mass growth.

claim: Mass production was not tightly coupled to volume growth.
source: Thus, mass production was not tightly coupled to volume growth.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the observations.

claim: The increase of density in mitosis and cytokinesis arises as consequence of continued mass accumulation when volume growth is halted.
source: These measurements suggest a simple model in which the increase of density in mitosis and cytokinesis arises as consequence of continued mass accumulation when volume growth is halted.
evidence: The results section proposes this model based on the measurements.

claim: In cdc25-22 cells during their prolonged G2 phase of 2–3 hr, intracellular density decreased further than in wild-type cells (~8% in cdc25-22 cells from 267 ± 19 to 245 ± 6 mg/mL, compared to ~5% in wild-type cells from 267 ± 11 to 250 ± 6 mg/mL).
source: In these mutant cells, during their prolonged G2 phase of 2–3 hr, intracellular density decreased further than in wild-type cells (~8% in cdc25-22 cells from 267 ± 19 to 245 ± 6 mg/mL, compared to ~5% in wild-type cells from 267 ± 11 to 250 ± 6 mg/mL) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: No evidence of density oscillations in the prolonged G2 phase was evident.
source: No evidence of density oscillations in the prolonged G2 phase was evident, arguing against cell-cycle independent oscillations as the cause of density variations during a normal cell cycle.
evidence: The results section reports this negative finding.

claim: Density falls during G2 phase because the rate of volume growth continues to be slightly faster than the rate of biosynthesis.
source: These data suggest that density falls during G2 phase because the rate of volume growth continues to be slightly faster than the rate of biosynthesis.
evidence: The results section infers this mechanism from the cdc25 experiments.

claim: At the non-permissive temperature, the mitotic interval was longer for cut7-446 cells (20–30 min) than for wild-type cells (10–20 min).
source: As expected, at the non-permissive temperature this interval was longer for cut7-446 cells (20–30 min) than for wild-type cells (10–20 min; Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: During the mitotic period, the density of wild-type and cut7-446 cells increased at a similar rate.
source: During this mitotic period, the density of wild-type and cut7-446 cells increased at a similar rate (Figure 4B,C): hence, the extended time in metaphase in cut7-446 cells led to a greater density increase (7% in cut7-446 from 270 ± 12 to 288 ± 14 mg/mL versus 5% in wild-type cells from 264 ± 11 to 278 ± 13 mg/mL).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: The extended time in metaphase in cut7-446 cells led to a greater density increase (7% in cut7-446 from 270 ± 12 to 288 ± 14 mg/mL versus 5% in wild-type cells from 264 ± 11 to 278 ± 13 mg/mL).
source: During this mitotic period, the density of wild-type and cut7-446 cells increased at a similar rate (Figure 4B,C): hence, the extended time in metaphase in cut7-446 cells led to a greater density increase (7% in cut7-446 from 270 ± 12 to 288 ± 14 mg/mL versus 5% in wild-type cells from 264 ± 11 to 278 ± 13 mg/mL).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: cdc16-116 mutant cells arrest in cytokinesis at the restrictive temperature, and thus repeatedly make septa without elongating.
source: cdc16-116 mutant cells arrest in cytokinesis at the restrictive temperature, and thus repeatedly make septa without elongating (Minet et al., 1979).
evidence: The results section cites Minet et al., 1979 for this mutant phenotype.

claim: Upon a shift from 25°C to the non-permissive temperature (34°C), cdc16 cells that maintained cytokinetic arrest continued to increase in cytoplasmic density; density after 90 min was 20–30% higher than in cytokinesis-competent wild-type cells.
source: Upon a shift from 25°C to the non-permissive temperature (34°C), cells that maintained cytokinetic arrest continued to increase in cytoplasmic density; density after 90 min was 20–30% higher than in cytokinesis-competent wild-type cells (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Biosynthesis continues throughout an extended block of mitosis or cytokinesis, leading to abnormally high intracellular density.
source: Thus, biosynthesis continues throughout an extended block of mitosis or cytokinesis, leading to abnormally high intracellular density.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the cell cycle arrest experiments.

claim: Latrunculin A treatment causes immediate cessation of tip growth independent of cell-cycle stage.
source: However, since these treatments do not completely halt volume growth and/or result in cell death, we treated wild-type cells with the F-actin inhibitor latrunculin A, which causes immediate cessation of tip growth independent of cell-cycle stage (Pan et al., 2014; Mutavchiev et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section cites Pan et al., 2014 and Mutavchiev et al., 2016 for this effect.

claim: QPI density maps showed that latrunculin A treatment caused all cells to immediately halt tip growth and begin to steadily increase in density, regardless of cell-cycle stage.
source: QPI density maps showed that latrunculin A treatment caused all cells to immediately halt tip growth and begin to steadily increase in density, regardless of cell-cycle stage (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: The mean density increase after 1 hr of latrunculin A treatment was ~20%.
source: The mean density increase after 1 hr was ~20% (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Mass increases were variable and on average increased more slowly during latrunculin A treatment than during normal growth.
source: However, we noted that in contrast to the mitotic and cytokinesis arrests, mass increases were variable and on average increased more slowly during latrunculin A treatment than during normal growth (Figure 5B, Figure 2D), suggesting a partial slowdown in biosynthesis and/or an increase in degradation.
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Mass increases during latrunculin A treatment suggest a partial slowdown in biosynthesis and/or an increase in degradation.
source: However, we noted that in contrast to the mitotic and cytokinesis arrests, mass increases were variable and on average increased more slowly during latrunculin A treatment than during normal growth (Figure 5B, Figure 2D), suggesting a partial slowdown in biosynthesis and/or an increase in degradation.
evidence: The results section infers this from the mass measurements.

claim: Cell density differences are exacerbated during cell cycle arrests.
source: Taken together, these results show that cell density differences are exacerbated during cell cycle arrests and that inhibition of volume growth is sufficient to increase intracellular density.
evidence: The results section summarizes findings from cell cycle arrest experiments.

claim: Inhibition of volume growth is sufficient to increase intracellular density.
source: Taken together, these results show that cell density differences are exacerbated during cell cycle arrests and that inhibition of volume growth is sufficient to increase intracellular density.
evidence: The results section summarizes findings from latrunculin A experiments.

claim: The variations in intracellular density arise from cell-cycle-dependent changes in volume growth rate.
source: Rather, our results strongly support a model in which the variations in intracellular density arise from cell-cycle-dependent changes in volume growth rate.
evidence: The results section concludes this model from the experiments.

claim: After cell division, the old end initiates tip growth soon after cell birth, and partway through G2, tip growth at the new end begins, but at a slower rate than the old end (or not all).
source: Fission yeast cells have a well-known pattern of volume growth in which after cell division, the old end initiates tip growth soon after cell birth, and partway through G2, tip growth at the new end begins, but at a slower rate than the old end (or not all) (Mitchison and Nurse, 1985; Chang and Martin, 2009).
evidence: The results section cites Mitchison and Nurse, 1985 and Chang and Martin, 2009 for this pattern.

claim: The old and new ends grew over the course of the cycle on average by ~4 and 2 µm, respectively.
source: As expected, our time-lapse data showed that the old and new ends grew over the course of the cycle on average by ~4 and 2 µm, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports this measurement.

claim: Many cells exhibited a gradient of intracellular density in which the ends that were actively growing appeared less dense than the non-growing ends.
source: In QPI density maps, we noted that many cells exhibited a gradient of intracellular density in which the ends that were actively growing appeared less dense than the non-growing ends (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The slower-growing new end typically appeared denser than the faster-growing end.
source: We hypothesized that these subcellular gradients reflected differences in tip growth between the two ends of the cell. In agreement with our hypothesis, the slower-growing new end typically appeared denser than the faster-growing end (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: In some cells, the difference in densities between the fast- and slow-growing ends was ~10% of the mean overall density.
source: In some cells, the difference in densities between the fast- and slow-growing ends was ~10% of the mean overall density (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The mean density difference between the two ends throughout the cell cycle was ~15 mg/mL, corresponding to ~5% of the mean overall density.
source: The mean density difference between the two ends throughout the cell cycle was ~15 mg/mL, corresponding to ~5% of the mean overall density (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section reports this measurement with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Local density and tip growth remained highly correlated even when analysis was constrained to cells within a narrow range of widths.
source: To address the potential for differences in the widths (and hence heights above the coverslip) of old and new ends to influence phase shifts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), we constrained our analysis to cells within a narrow range of widths and found that local density and tip growth remained highly correlated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section reports this control analysis with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: FITC intensity differed by ~5% between the old and new end of monopolar cells that are growing only from the old end.
source: We further confirmed the presence of spatial gradients by staining cells for total protein and RNA using the dye fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC). FITC intensity differed by ~5% between the old and new end of monopolar cells that are growing only from the old end (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), consistent with the gradient in QPI density maps.
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: In cells treated with latrunculin A, spatial density gradients persisted over time.
source: Since tip growth is regulated by actin-dependent mechanisms (Pan et al., 2014; Mutavchiev et al., 2016; Chang and Martin, 2009), we tested whether maintenance of the gradient is dependent on F-actin or tip growth: we found that in cells treated with latrunculin A, spatial density gradients persisted over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Intracellular density gradients are stable and linked to local growth patterns.
source: These results demonstrate that intracellular density gradients are stable and linked to local growth patterns, and that their maintenance does not require active growth or F-actin.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the latrunculin A experiments.

claim: The maintenance of intracellular density gradients does not require active growth or F-actin.
source: These results demonstrate that intracellular density gradients are stable and linked to local growth patterns, and that their maintenance does not require active growth or F-actin.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the latrunculin A experiments.

claim: Time-lapse imaging showed that the intracellular density differences established during interphase were often propagated through cell division and correlated with density differences between the progeny daughter cells after cytokinesis.
source: Time-lapse imaging showed that the intracellular density differences established during interphase were often propagated through cell division and correlated with density differences between the progeny daughter cells after cytokinesis (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Subcellular density variations are stable enough to be propagated through generations.
source: Thus, subcellular density variations are stable enough to be propagated through generations.
evidence: The results section concludes this from the time-lapse observations.

claim: The septum between daughter cells generally bent away from the more dense compartment.
source: As noted above, the densities of daughter compartments in septated cells were often different from each other (Figure 6D,E); these differences were often exacerbated in cells with cell-division defects, such as mid1, mid2, and cdc16 cells. We noted that the septum between these daughter cells generally bent away from the more dense compartment (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section reports this observation with reference to figures.

claim: The septum is an elastic structure that can be used as a biosensor that reports on osmotic pressure differences between compartments.
source: Previous studies (Atilgan et al., 2015) reported that the septum is an elastic structure that can be used as a biosensor that reports on osmotic pressure differences between compartments.
evidence: The results section cites Atilgan et al., 2015 for this property.

claim: When one daughter is lysed by laser microsurgery and loses turgor pressure, the septum bulges away from the intact daughter.
source: For instance, when one daughter is lysed by laser microsurgery and loses turgor pressure, the septum bulges away from the intact daughter (Atilgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites Atilgan et al., 2015 for this observation.

claim: Temporal fluctuations in septum bending have been proposed to arise from fluctuations in pressure differences between daughter cells.
source: Temporal fluctuations in septum bending have been proposed to arise from fluctuations in pressure differences between daughter cells (Muñoz et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites Muñoz et al., 2013 for this proposal.

claim: Of the 71% (64/90) of mid2∆ cells exhibiting a bent septum, 97% (62/64) exhibited a septum bent away from the compartment of higher density at the time of maximum density difference.
source: Of the 71% (64/90) of cells exhibiting a bent septum, 97% (62/64) exhibited a septum bent away from the compartment of higher density at the time of maximum density difference (Figure 7A), with a mean maximum difference of 16 ± 5% (Figure 7B).
evidence: The results section reports this quantitative observation with reference to figures.

claim: The mean maximum density difference in mid2∆ cells with bent septa was 16 ± 5%.
source: Of the 71% (64/90) of cells exhibiting a bent septum, 97% (62/64) exhibited a septum bent away from the compartment of higher density at the time of maximum density difference (Figure 7A), with a mean maximum difference of 16 ± 5% (Figure 7B).
evidence: The results section reports this measurement with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: In instances where the septum appeared flat, the density difference was substantially lower (~4.5%) than in cells with a bent septum.
source: In instances where the septum appeared flat, the density difference was substantially lower (~4.5%) than in cells with a bent septum.
evidence: The results section reports this observation.

claim: Septal bending occurred for density differences as low as 5–10%.
source: The observation that septal bending occurred for density differences as low as 5–10% suggests that the density variations over the course of a normal cell cycle (Figure 2), in cell cycle-arrested cells (Figures 3, 4 and 5) or between growing and non-growing cell tips (Figure 6) may reflect substantial changes in turgor-mediated stresses.
evidence: The results section reports this observation.

claim: The density variations over the course of a normal cell cycle, in cell cycle-arrested cells, or between growing and non-growing cell tips may reflect substantial changes in turgor-mediated stresses.
source: The observation that septal bending occurred for density differences as low as 5–10% suggests that the density variations over the course of a normal cell cycle (Figure 2), in cell cycle-arrested cells (Figures 3, 4 and 5) or between growing and non-growing cell tips (Figure 6) may reflect substantial changes in turgor-mediated stresses.
evidence: The results section infers this from the septal bending observations.

claim: Exponential-phase fission yeast cells have a dry-mass density of 282 ± 16 mg/mL.
source: Here, we established a QPI method based on z-stacks of bright-field images for quantifying intracellular density dynamics in living cells. We found that exponential-phase fission yeast cells have a dry-mass density of 282 ± 16 mg/mL (Figure 1C–E) and a buoyant-mass density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL (Figure 2E), comparable to measurements in other organisms (Neurohr and Amon, 2020; Bryan et al., 2010).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main findings with reference to figures.

claim: Exponential-phase fission yeast cells have a buoyant-mass density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL.
source: Here, we established a QPI method based on z-stacks of bright-field images for quantifying intracellular density dynamics in living cells. We found that exponential-phase fission yeast cells have a dry-mass density of 282 ± 16 mg/mL (Figure 1C–E) and a buoyant-mass density of 1.108 ± 0.005 g/mL (Figure 2E), comparable to measurements in other organisms (Neurohr and Amon, 2020; Bryan et al., 2010).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main findings with reference to Figure 2E.

evidence: The discussion cites Neurohr and Amon, 2020 and Bryan et al., 2010 for comparison.

claim: Density varied systematically across the cell cycle in wild-type fission yeast cells over a range of ~10%.
source: Density varied systematically across the cell cycle in wild-type fission yeast cells over a range of ~10% (Figure 2C), while the relative rate of dry-mass synthesis remained constant (reflecting exponential accumulation) throughout all cell-cycle stages (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings with reference to figures.

claim: These quantitative findings are consistent with more qualitative density studies of fission yeast using other methods.
source: These quantitative findings, which utilize precise sub-pixel measurements of cellular dimensions and automated analysis platforms, are consistent with more qualitative density studies of fission yeast using other methods (Rappaz et al., 2009; Mitchison, 1957; Stonyte et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion cites Rappaz et al., 2009, Mitchison, 1957, and Stonyte et al., 2018 for comparison.

claim: Volume growth and biosynthesis were not tightly coupled throughout the cell cycle.
source: Accordingly, volume growth and biosynthesis were not tightly coupled throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: The discussion concludes this from the data.

claim: cdc25 mutants delayed in G2 phase exhibited a steady decline in density as cells elongated abnormally.
source: Consistent with this model, density shifts were exacerbated by perturbations of cell-cycle progression or of volume growth directly. cdc25 mutants delayed in G2 phase exhibited a steady decline in density as cells elongated abnormally (Figure 3), reminiscent of the cytoplasmic dilution observed in very enlarged budding yeast cells and senescent mammalian cells (Neurohr et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The density decline in cdc25 mutants is reminiscent of the cytoplasmic dilution observed in very enlarged budding yeast cells and senescent mammalian cells.
source: Consistent with this model, density shifts were exacerbated by perturbations of cell-cycle progression or of volume growth directly. cdc25 mutants delayed in G2 phase exhibited a steady decline in density as cells elongated abnormally (Figure 3), reminiscent of the cytoplasmic dilution observed in very enlarged budding yeast cells and senescent mammalian cells (Neurohr et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites Neurohr et al., 2019 for comparison.

claim: During mitotic arrest at the spindle checkpoint (cut7) or cytokinesis arrest through regulation of the SIN pathway (cdc16), volume growth was slowed but mass synthesis was unaffected, resulting in steady density increases.
source: During mitotic arrest at the spindle checkpoint (cut7) or cytokinesis arrest through regulation of the SIN pathway (cdc16), volume growth was slowed but mass synthesis was unaffected, resulting in steady density increases (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings with reference to figures.

claim: Inhibition of cell growth with latrunculin A caused a steady increase in density regardless of cell-cycle stage.
source: Inhibition of cell growth with latrunculin A caused a steady increase in density regardless of cell-cycle stage (Figure 5).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Any perturbation that affects cell-cycle progression or growth is likely to alter density dynamics.
source: These findings suggest that any perturbation that affects cell-cycle progression or growth is likely to alter density dynamics.
evidence: The discussion infers this general principle from the experiments.

claim: Cell-cycle arrests are commonly used to synchronize cells and are often triggered in response to stresses such as DNA damage.
source: Cell-cycle arrests are commonly used to synchronize cells and are often triggered in response to stresses such as DNA damage.
evidence: The discussion states this as common knowledge.

claim: Cell-cycle arrests not only affect cell-cycle progression and cell size, but also cause changes in intracellular density and potentially other downstream changes in physiology.
source: Our study demonstrates that such perturbations are not as innocuous as often thought; arrests not only affect cell-cycle progression and cell size, but also cause changes in intracellular density and potentially other downstream changes in physiology.
evidence: The discussion concludes this from the study findings.

claim: Mass accumulation was continuous in fission yeast, consistent with previous studies.
source: We found that mass accumulation was continuous, consistent with previous studies (Mitchison, 1957; Stonyte et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion cites Mitchison, 1957 and Stonyte et al., 2018 for consistency.

claim: Mass dynamics were exponential in nature, consistent with findings in other cell types.
source: Notably, our quantitative measurements suggested that mass dynamics were exponential in nature (Figure 2D,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), consistent with findings in other cell types (Godin et al., 2010).

claim: In budding yeast, buoyant density is lowest in early G1 and rises in late G1 and S phase at the time of bud formation.
source: In budding yeast, buoyant density is lowest in early G1 and rises in late G1 and S phase at the time of bud formation (Bryan et al., 2010).
evidence: The discussion cites Bryan et al., 2010 for this observation in budding yeast.

claim: Cell-cycle arrests in S and M phase and latrunculin A treatment do not lead to increases in buoyant density in budding yeast, unlike findings in fission yeast.
source: Moreover, cell-cycle arrests in S and M phase and latrunculin A treatment do not lead to increases in buoyant density in budding yeast, unlike our findings in fission yeast (Figure 5).
evidence: The discussion contrasts findings in budding yeast with fission yeast.

claim: In human cells, mass growth continues in early mitosis, but stops in metaphase and resumes in late cytokinesis, potentially with subtle oscillations.
source: In human cells, mass growth continues in early mitosis, but stops in metaphase and resumes in late cytokinesis, potentially with subtle oscillations (Liu et al., 2020; Miettinen et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites Liu et al., 2020 and Miettinen et al., 2019 for this observation in human cells.

claim: Density is constant in human cells during much of the cell cycle, but decreases in mitosis (by 0.5% in buoyant mass, equivalent to >10% decrease in dry-mass density) coincident with a 10–30% volume increase during mitotic rounding; density then slightly increases in cytokinesis.
source: Density is constant in human cells during much of the cell cycle, but decreases in mitosis (by 0.5% in buoyant mass, equivalent to >10% decrease in dry-mass density) coincident with a 10–30% volume increase during mitotic rounding; density then slightly increases in cytokinesis (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion cites Son et al., 2015 and Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015 for this observation in human cells.

claim: In the bacterium Escherichia coli, density varies somewhat from birth to division, but the ratio of surface area to mass is relatively constant, suggesting that biosynthesis is linked to surface-area synthesis.
source: In the bacterium Escherichia coli, density varies somewhat from birth to division, but the ratio of surface area to mass is relatively constant, suggesting that biosynthesis is linked to surface-area synthesis (Oldewurtel et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites Oldewurtel et al., 2019 for this observation in E. coli.

claim: In fission yeast, mass was more closely coupled with surface area than volume, especially when the surface area of both sides of the septum were factored in.
source: Here, we found that in fission yeast, mass was also more closely coupled with surface area than volume, especially when the surface area of both sides of the septum were factored in (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: The discussion reports this finding with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Examples such as latruculin A-treated cells demonstrated that mass accumulation and surface area growth are not inextricably linked and can be uncoupled.
source: However, examples such as latruculin A-treated cells (Figure 5B) demonstrated that mass accumulation and surface area growth are not inextricably linked and can be uncoupled.
evidence: The discussion concludes this from the latrunculin A experiments.

claim: Tip growth involves the extension and assembly of new cell wall and plasma membrane at the growing tip.
source: Fission yeast cells grow through tip growth, which involves the extension and assembly of new cell wall and plasma membrane at the growing tip; this growth is accomplished by a complex integration of the cell-polarity machinery, exocytosis, wall growth and mechanics, and turgor pressure (Martin and Arkowitz, 2014; Chang and Martin, 2009).
evidence: The discussion cites Martin and Arkowitz, 2014 and Chang and Martin, 2009 for this description.

claim: Tip growth is accomplished by a complex integration of the cell-polarity machinery, exocytosis, wall growth and mechanics, and turgor pressure.
source: Fission yeast cells grow through tip growth, which involves the extension and assembly of new cell wall and plasma membrane at the growing tip; this growth is accomplished by a complex integration of the cell-polarity machinery, exocytosis, wall growth and mechanics, and turgor pressure (Martin and Arkowitz, 2014; Chang and Martin, 2009).
evidence: The discussion cites Martin and Arkowitz, 2014 and Chang and Martin, 2009 for this description.

claim: Polarized patterns have been detected in immunofluorescence of damaged (carbonylated) proteins, which may impact replicative aging.
source: We note that polarized patterns have been detected in immunofluorescence of damaged (carbonylated) proteins, which may impact replicative aging (Erjavec et al., 2008).

claim: Spatial heterogeneities in density have also been observed in mammalian cells.
source: Spatial heterogeneities in density have also been observed in mammalian cells; it remains to be determined whether these patterns are related to cell shape, organelles, or variations in cytoplasmic density (Oh et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2007; Tolde et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion cites Oh et al., 2019, Choi et al., 2007, and Tolde et al., 2018 for this observation.

claim: The density changes of 5–20% could have profound consequences for the biochemistry of cellular reactions and on macromolecular crowding and viscosity.
source: The density changes of 5–20% that we observed, which likely affect the concentration of most if not all cellular components in the cytoplasm, could have profound consequences for the biochemistry of cellular reactions and on macromolecular crowding and viscosity, for instance through effects on diffusion (Mitchison, 2019; Neurohr et al., 2019; van den Berg et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2008; Luby-Phelps, 2000).
evidence: The discussion cites multiple references for potential consequences of density changes.

claim: The observed density variations may signify cell-cycle-dependent and spatial changes in the physical properties of the cytoplasm.
source: An intriguing implication of our findings is that the observed density variations may signify cell-cycle-dependent and spatial changes in the physical properties of the cytoplasm.

claim: Intracellular osmotic pressure and density differences between daughter compartments were strongly coupled, as evidenced by bending of the elastic septal cell wall.
source: Here, we provided evidence that density also affects cell mechanics and thereby influence cell shape. Intracellular osmotic pressure and density differences between daughter compartments were strongly coupled, as evidenced by bending of the elastic septal cell wall (Figure 7).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the findings with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Density may affect pressure through effects on macromolecular crowding, which produces colloid osmotic pressure associated with the displacement of water.
source: Density may affect pressure through effects on macromolecular crowding, which produces colloid osmotic pressure associated with the displacement of water (Mitchison, 2019).

claim: Differences in colloid osmotic pressure have been proposed to influence nuclear size.
source: Differences in colloid osmotic pressure have been proposed to influence nuclear size (Mitchison, 2019; Harding and Feldherr, 1959), but experimental evidence linking crowding to force generation in vivo generally remains scant.
evidence: The discussion cites Mitchison, 2019 and Harding and Feldherr, 1959 for this proposal.

claim: The findings lend important support to the idea that different densities of macromolecules can generate large enough differences in colloid osmotic pressure to alter cell shape.

claim: The increase of density at cell division may provide mechanical force through increased turgor pressure to facilitate cell-cell separation and bulging of the cell wall.
source: We speculate that the increase of density at cell division may provide mechanical force through increased turgor pressure to facilitate cell-cell separation and bulging of the cell wall (Atilgan et al., 2015), and may affect the distribution of mechanical stresses within the cell wall during other cell-cycle stages as well.
evidence: The discussion speculates on this mechanism and cites Atilgan et al., 2015.

claim: Density increase at cell division may affect the distribution of mechanical stresses within the cell wall during other cell-cycle stages.
